While Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods have been widely employed to sample configurational sampling in molecular systems, recent studies suggest that dynamical approaches, specifically the Langevin Dynamics (LD), could offer superior performance. This work examines the practical feasibility of LD, a technique originally developed in chemical physics, for molecular modeling. We provide a detailed analysis of LD's theoretical and actual sampling efficiency, comparing it directly with Metropolis-Hastings (MH) algorithms. Additionally, we outline potential applications of LD in molecular dynamics simulations and suggest strategies for enhancing the efficiency of both LD and MH. To validate these concepts, the paper presents detailed sampling trials on a Lennard-Jones system and a peptide, demonstrating that LD can significantly outperform standard MH and conventional Langevin dynamics simulations in terms of sampling efficiency. Specifically, our results indicate that optimized LD parameters can yield sampling rates up to 50 times greater than those achieved with conventional simulation protocols. Despite this significant improvement, further increases in efficiency prove difficult, as the optimal friction coefficient depends on the specific system under study and its initial kinetic energy. Although LD demonstrates high efficiency, it introduces non-local modifications to the target distribution; however, these deviations are minimal when the friction coefficient is appropriately selected. Consequently, LD emerges as a robust and efficient algorithm for sampling molecular configurations, potentially serving as a valuable alternative to MD simulations, particularly when time-resolved details are unnecessary. To facilitate this, we have released an open-source C++ codebase for LD, available at https://github.com/huajust/LD. This implementation includes a Metropolis-accelerated variant, confirming that the MH step adds negligible overhead even with small proposal distributions. Furthermore, the code supports "global" movement proposals, which, when combined with global optimization methods like simulated annealing or parallel tempering, can dramatically improve sampling—especially for systems facing rugged energy landscapes. Beyond optimized configurational sampling, the LD framework can also support dynamic simulations; by tuning the friction coefficient to match the desired timescale, one can explore dynamics up to the diffusive limit, although the resulting samples will reflect the nonphysical friction introduced into the equations of motion. In summary, this study highlights the efficacy of LD for both optimized configurational sampling and dynamic simulation, providing a flexible tool for researchers to select the most appropriate sampling strategy for their specific requirements. Nonlocal gravity models serve as effective frameworks for accounting for anomalous acceleration effects in astrophysical systems without invoking extra dimensions, string theories, or dark matter. Although these models are phenomenological and lack a fundamental theoretical basis, they offer valuable insights into the source of gravitational nonlocality. This paper introduces a constitutive formulation for nonlocal gravity, drawing an analogy with constitutive approaches in classical and relativistic nonlocal media. Within this framework, the constitutive tensor responsible for nonlocality functions as a fundamental variable, while the gravitational field tensor (Riemann) acts as the background constituent tensor. We demonstrate that, similar to electromagnetism, multiple constitutive tensors can coexist. Furthermore, we establish that anisotropic inertia arises naturally from this nonlocal constitutive tensor and constitutes a hitherto unrecognized property of spacetime. Our derivation shows that the constitutive tensor possesses a mathematical structure identical to that of a Riemann tensor, supporting the hypothesis that nonlocality and curvature share the same underlying mechanism. Consequently, the constitutive tensor can be viewed as a "Riemann tensor at a distance," enabling us to define a nonlocal connection (Riemann- like) and subsequently a nonlocal metric (Cartan- like). Notably, this metric is nonlocal with respect to the Minkowski background but remains local relative to itself, giving rise to a hierarchical structure of nonlocality. We further illustrate how this nonlocal metric induces coordinate transformations in the GR constitutive tensor (Weyl), thereby generating a nonlocal Weyl tensor and a corresponding nonlocal Einstein tensor. Ultimately, we conclude that a nonlocal Einstein- like tensor and a nonlocal constitutive tensor are unnecessary for describing gravitational phenomena.

We analyze the variable quenching of thermal X-ray flares from point sources in the Milky Way's central bulge and sphere of influence. While prior studies attributed these fluctuations to the intermittent nature of the transients, we demonstrate that the intervals between flare repetitions are determined by the stars' orbital motions. Specifically, the flares occur twice per orbit as the neutron star's accretion disk alternates between visibility and occultation by the companion star. Using the measured flare intervals, we estimate the orbital periods for seven transient systems with identifiable repetition intervals. For four systems where the interval is short enough to serve as an upper limit on the orbital period, we calculate lower bounds for their periods. We find that all seven systems with determined or limit-based periods exhibit unusually long periods, averaging $5.6\times$ longer than the typical $2$h observed for known Galactic dwarf and intermediate-mass X-ray binaries. Consequently, the presence of an X-ray flare does not guarantee that a point source's orbital period falls within the current observational sample of $\lesssim10$h. Based on these results, we propose a classification for dormant neutron star X-ray binary systems in the Milky Way's bulge and central sphere of influence into two groups: those with observable flare-powered transients having periods $\lesssim20$h, and those with undetectable non-flaring transients or permanently quenching accretion disks, also constrained to periods of $\lesssim20$h. We conclude by outlining the unique characteristics of these systems and suggesting potential strategies to uncover the orbital periods and other properties of their non-flaring transients. This work serves as a companion to /2405.16004/, and we utilize the derived orbital periods to investigate the future awakening of these systems.

High-frequency CPU architectures deliver superior performance, yet they entail elevated costs, greater power consumption, and enhanced vulnerability to failures and attacks. This paper introduces HyperDegrade, a systematic co-design of compilation techniques and hardware degradation strategies that enables high-performance low-frequency CPUs to match the efficacy of low-performance high-frequency counterparts. Experimental results with high-language workloads demonstrate that a 1.5x frequency reduction yields a nearly identical performance to a 2x frequency decrease, while a 3x reduction still maintains a 1.6x performance relative to the original high frequency. These findings indicate that compilation-level parallelism optimizations can compensate for reduced hardware frequency to sustain performance. Beyond performance goals, HyperDegrade allows CPU frequency to be treated as a configurable parameter to satisfy specific constraints, such as power limits, fault-tolerance requirements, DDoS defense, and side-channel attack mitigation, without compromising performance targets. Introducing frequency degradation as an on-the-fly defense mechanism, our experiments show that shifting from 3GHz to 1GHz under a DoS attack provides a 1.6x improvement, and moving to 500MHz offers an additional 1.2x gain. Furthermore, HyperDegrade can serve as a countermeasure against Cache-based side-channel attacks like Spectre; under workloads constrained by execution time, frequency degradation delivered a 2x to 4x improvement against Spectre vulnerabilities compared to the original configuration. Additional experiments confirm that this approach remains effective even when execution time limits are relaxed. The core design of HyperDegrade involves multi-granularity optimizations at both hardware and compilation layers: at the hardware level, register files and caches are shrunk, and compile-time scheduling optimizations are applied; at the compilation level, loop unrolling is reduced, basic block sizes are limited, and innovative "sacrifice" optimizations are implemented to maximize performance under the adjusted hardware specifications. Under workloads with execution time constraints, our experiments establish that frequency degradation provides a positive defensive effect against such attacks, and this benefit extends to other concurrent attacks, suggesting a cumulative defensive advantage. The detection of astrophysical gravitational waves (GWs) relies on extending the effective sensing range beyond the LIGO-style interferometer's characteristic triangular peak, which typically occurs around 900 Hz. To achieve this, novel architectural modifications are required. Although Sagnac interferometers are commonly utilized for inertial navigation due to their high-frequency gain, their narrow bandwidth has limited their adoption for GW detection. This manuscript introduces a non-reciprocal sloshing-Sagnac interferometer configuration designed to maximize both bandwidth and sensitivity. Theoretical models and simulations of this design are compared against the second-generation LIGO (LIGO-II) architecture. Simulated strain spectral density curves demonstrate that the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer could exhibit a 4.4 decibel higher sensitivity at 2.2 kHz and a 7.1 decibel improvement at 5.1 kHz relative to plus-oriented LIGO-II. Furthermore, when integrated with the seismically isolated mirror masses of GW detectors, the inertial sensing bandwidth of a sloshing-Sagnac interferometer could exceed 100 kHz, delivering superior sensitivity within this high-frequency range. Among the most critical hyperparameters for neural networks, the choice of loss function is both among the most difficult to set and the least commonly optimized. Despite this, existing studies examining its impact on a specific network architecture remain scarce. This work conducts a comprehensive analysis of various loss functions for both classified regression and classification tasks. While conventional approaches typically combine a primary loss with an auxiliary loss (such as accuracy) using a weighted sum, a significant challenge arises in adapting these methods for categorical problems, which requires a specialized formulation. Ultimately, our empirical results demonstrate that for classification tasks, the Mean Error loss—when paired with a suitable optimization algorithm—consistently outperforms all other tested losses, yielding the lowest validation scores and superior performance relative to other architectures. In contrast, for multi-class classification problems, Cross Entropy remains the optimal choice. These findings hold true regardless of data size or the specific problem domain, applying universally to supervised classification and multi-task regression issues. Notably, these conclusions are drawn without introducing any novel network structures; the improvements stem solely from altering the loss function. Given these results, the industry should reconsider its standard use of Cross Entropy for multi-label classification and Mean Squared Error for other classification and multi-task regression problems. Our analysis indicates that the Mean Absolute Error function is actually the most effective loss for such multi-class scenarios. Furthermore, we observed that in certain multi-class problems, the Signed Absolute Error performed even better than Mean Absolute Error, though this varies by dataset. For those same datasets, neither Cross Entropy nor Mean Squared Error produced optimal outcomes. Additionally, the order of class labeling in one-hot encoding did not affect performance with Cross Entropy, but it significantly influenced results for error-based losses like Mean Absolute Error and Signed Absolute Error. As a final recommendation, researchers and practitioners should avoid combining multiple loss functions for standard classification or multi-task regression problems, as the dominant loss determines the network's focus, leaving other objectives underprioritized. Instead, a single, appropriately selected loss function should be utilized.

We introduce ATOMIC, an atlas of machine-commonsense knowledge comprising approximately 287,000 entries that enable if-then inference. This structure facilitates the rapid retrieval of facts regarding agents, events, and situations. In contrast to recent work focusing on retrieving multiple parallel reasoned actions for a specific situation (situation reasoning), our if-then inference approach supports more complex logical deductions, such as inferring that a sandwich is edible if it has been buttered and toasted. To achieve this, we utilize a syntax for if-then relations similar to the ACT knowledge graph (Branavan et al., 2011). ATOMIC covers three domains: actions (205,414 if-then relations), events (50,084), and situations (31,000). Furthermore, we demonstrate that language models can acquire knowledge of these if-then relations and that humans can readily follow them to predict subsequent actions or events. At a technical level, our if-then inference syntax is more expressive than previous graph-based approaches for representing common sense knowledge, and we show that neural models can learn this syntax without losing performance on language understanding tasks. The metric dimension of a graph represents the minimum required for a vertices set to function as a resolving set. This concept has been extensively analyzed using graph theory to establish various characteristics of the associated function and to explore potential applications within distance metric geometry. Alternatively, one can define a metric dimension for finite graphs based on a distinct metric: the induced metric from a finite, symmetric distance function that satisfies the triangle inequality and posits that adjacent vertices are exactly distance one apart, without necessitating that the distance between any pair of vertices is an integer. This alternative dimension aligns with the traditional metric dimension when considering graphs under their standard metric. Consequently, this paper investigates the properties of this revised metric dimension for finite graphs, utilizing the term "compressed metric dimension" to describe it. The study involves analyzing its fundamental attributes, determining bounds, and exploring how it varies with respect to specific graph operations and induced subgraphs. Furthermore, the research establishes a formula for the compressed metric dimension of the join of two graphs and investigates its characteristics for trees, cycles, and graphs constrained by diameter and maximum degree. Alongside the demonstration of these higher ordered methods on a GPU for linear inversion, this work also presents a novel iterative approach on a CPU that achieves a 50-fold faster convergence than traditional CG methods. This paper examines the one-dimensional focusing energy-critical nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation defined on the exterior of a convex barrier, which features Neumann boundary conditions. We demonstrate that the dynamics near the ground state are deterministic and that scattering occurs for initial energies strictly below the threshold corresponding to a specific explosive solution. Additionally, we analyze the deterministic dynamics and uniqueness of solutions for high-energy initial data. In particular, we establish the existence of explosive solutions that focus at a positive time on the boundary of the convex barrier and become singular in the boundary layer without changing shape. These findings generalize previous results obtained for Schr\"odinger equations on domains with strictly convex boundaries. Generalizing the model to a non-convex barrier, we prove that explosions occur for any initial data with positive semi-norm exceeding a specific threshold, regardless of energy level. Furthermore, we show that global solutions exist when the $L^2$-norm remains sufficiently small.

This study presents a methodology for effectively analyzing Bayes factors within specific statistical frameworks to draw conclusion-level inferences about hypothesis testing. The approach involves computing Bayes factors for multiple pairs of nested and non-nested models to evaluate three distinct inference categories: strong evidence for $H_1$, moderate evidence favoring $H_1$ over $H_2$, and moderate or strong evidence in favor of neither set of hypotheses. A decision rule integrates these inferences with prior commitments regarding hypothesis pairs to finalize conclusion-level decisions. The proposed framework enables the strong endorsement of complex model structures, shifts evidence between competing hypotheses, and combines such evidence with prior stakes to form final conclusions. Additionally, the decision rule offers a flexible, semi-quantitative mechanism for assigning weights to different evidence types among stakeholders who may hold varying prior beliefs about model pairs. Practical applications demonstrate how this methodology supports final conclusion-level inferences, particularly for regulatory bodies evaluating complex model nesting and prior commitments. For organizational entities with specific stakeholder priorities, the decision rule allows for tailored adjustments to prioritize certain hypothesis pairs over others. Finally, the article introduces a set of workflow strategies required to strongly apply Bayes factors, addressing computational challenges inherent in calculating these metrics across complex models. A key contribution is a refined, symbolic version of the co-nesting level metric, which guides the search for solutions and ensures termination. The approach covers union, concatenation, and star operations on the right-hand side, as well as iteration, plus, and wildcard operations on the left-hand side. Experimental outcomes align with state-of-the-art methods and demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness in analyzing XSL-T schemas for regular expression operators. Additionally, the provided source code serves as a semantic testbed for ERL expressions and can be adapted to implement alternative resolution strategies. The algorithm's practical applications span the analysis of security protocols, compilation of semantic grammar rules into access policies, and the investigation of software behavior through regular expression constraints.

Deriving sufficient balanced positive samples remains a significant challenge when applying supervised learning to identify rare skin cancer types. To address this, we introduce a two-stage approach for classifying seven distinct skin cancer varieties. In the first stage, a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) is trained on the entirety of the dataset to discern general skin cancer types. During the second stage, an outlier detection model—comprising a CNN and a Fully Connected (FC) layer—is utilized to classify specific cancer varieties. Experimental results on the ISIC 2013 dataset demonstrate that this method outperforms existing approaches, achieving an AUC of 99.03%, 98.97%, and 98.95% for the CC, BSCC, and SSCC categories, respectively. Furthermore, the system identified the "Raly" and "Actinic Keratosis" (AK) categories as outliers within the dataset, aligning with actual category distributions. These findings indicate that the two-stage model not only effectively classifies rare skin cancers but also detects underrepresented categories, making it a beneficial tool for dermatologists to assist in diagnosis. Leveraging this principle, we prove that no invariant surfaces exist in the Lorenz system when modeled with fractional orders, thereby concluding that the classic chaotic attractor in the Lorenz system cannot persist under fractional-order conditions. We present the minimal extension to the simplest scoto-seesaw model capable of achieving a normal neutrino mass pattern via the 3F-1D mass hierarchy. Within this framework, the neutrino oscillation parameters, particularly the mixing angles and mass-squared differences, constrain the underlying mass scale to approximately 1.5 TeV. Our analysis reveals that coannihilation becomes significant near the 2rd seesaw mechanism scale, while resonant annihilation dominates when the direct right-handed neutrino mass is close to the half of its limit. We provide a comprehensive study of the model's phenomenology, including production mechanisms at hadron colliders, at ~1 TeV muon colliders, and in future fixed-target experiments, alongside the detectability of zero-mode neutrinoless double beta decay.
